title: Generosity
hookLine: a twenty with a sigh, or a five with a smile: which is the better gift?
tomorrow: what would you give away if it cost you nearly everything?

lines: A FIVE AND A KIND NOTE.
cards: A farewell card goes round the office with an envelope taped inside. One person drops in a twenty and sighs about it. Another drops in a five and writes something that makes the person leaving cry.
So what makes a gift a good one: the size, or something else? There's an old answer to that, and two very different traditions give a surprisingly similar one.

teach.b: This block is the ten perfections, the qualities a Buddha-to-be is said to bring to fullness over many lives, and in the Theravada list, giving comes first. The word is dana.
In a short talk in the Anguttara Nikaya, the Buddha describes the giver in three moments.

teach.h: GLAD BEFORE, BRIGHT DURING, CONTENT AFTER.
teach.b: Before giving, glad. While giving, the mind bright and settled. After giving, content, with no regret.
The gift is measured partly in the person giving it. Now a neighbor.

Paul, writing to the Christians at Corinth about a collection for the believers in Jerusalem, says it this way: "Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
Two very different texts, and both look at the giver's face, not only at the amount. Gladness counts. Grudging is its own kind of loss.
And here's the honest difference. For Paul, the reason runs through God, who loves the cheerful giver.
In the Buddha's talk there's no creator in the picture: the gladness belongs to the giver's own mind, and to what the act becomes, now and later.
The same gladness, with two different reasons underneath it.
Back to the envelope. The twenty still buys more cake. But the five with the kind note has all three moments in it.

how: Buddhists practice dana by offering food to monastics, supporting temples and giving to people in need; teachers point to the giver's gladness before, during and after the gift, as the Anguttara Nikaya describes.

o: a monthly tax paid to support the temple
giving freely, glad before, during and after
a vow to own nothing and live on alms

games.q: the giver's three moments, and a neighbor — tap the pairs.

s: a gift is judged only by its size
the Buddha's talk looks at the giver too: glad before, bright during, content after.
in the Theravada list of ten perfections, giving comes first
dana opens the list, before virtue and renunciation.
Paul's letter says to give as much as you can, even grudgingly
it says not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.

games.q: two classmates give to the same fundraiser. one gives a lot and complains all week; one gives a little and is glad for days. by the three moments, what's going on?
o: only the big gift counts; the gladness is a nice extra.
the money helps either way, but only the glad giver has all three moments.
neither counts, because they both told people about it.
games.why: the gift still does its good. the teaching adds that it's measured partly in the giver: glad before, bright during, content after.

practice: Bring to mind three things you could give today: an object, some time, a kind word. Choose the one you could give gladly, and stay with that gladness now, before anything has left your hands.
That's the first of the three moments, and it's already happening.

wordCard.voice: Dana: giving, the first of the ten perfections. Glad before, bright during, content after.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: giving, generosity, the first perfection.

carryVoice: Something to keep: give freely, and let the gladness come first. One perfection down, nine to come.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 6.37, Chalangadana Sutta (the donor's three factors: glad before giving, the mind confident while giving, satisfied after giving)

sources.q: Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.
